first_draft_paragraphs.text: IT was 2 p.m. on the afternoon of May 7, 1915. The _Lusitania_, struck by two torpedoes in succession, was sinking rapidly, and the women and children were being lined up for the boats. One girl stood alone, slightly apart. She was not more than eighteen. She did not seem afraid, and her grave, steadfast eyes looked straight ahead.

“I beg your pardon.” A man’s voice beside her made her turn. She had noticed him amongst the first-class passengers. There was a hint of mystery about him: he spoke to no one, and he looked over his shoulder with a swift, suspicious glance. Now he was greatly agitated, evidently in a state of overmastering fear. And yet he did not strike her as the kind of man who would be afraid to meet death!
He stood looking at her with a kind of desperate irresolution. “It must be!” he muttered to himself. “Yes--it is the only way.” Then aloud he said abruptly: “You are an American?”
The girl flushed. “I guess you’ve no right to ask such a thing! Of course I am!”
“I’ve got to trust some one--and it must be a woman.”

“Because of ‘women and children first.’” He lowered his voice. “I’m carrying papers--vitally important papers. They may make all the difference to the Allies. They’ve more chance with you than with me. Will you take them?”
The girl held out her hand.
“Wait--I must warn you. There may be a risk--if I’ve been followed. I don’t think I have, but one never knows. Have you the nerve to go through with it?”
The girl smiled. “I’ll go through with it all right. And I’m real proud to be chosen! What am I to do with them afterwards?”

“I’ll advertise in the personal column of the _Times_, beginning ‘Shipmate.’ At the end of three days if there’s nothing, take the packet to the American Embassy, and deliver it into the Ambassador’s own hands.”
He took her hand in his. “Good-bye. Good luck to you,” he said in a louder tone.
Her hand closed on the oilskin packet that had lain in his palm.
As the _Lusitania_ listed to starboard, the girl went forward to take her place in the boat.

original_source:
IT was 2 p.m. on the afternoon of May 7, 1915. The _Lusitania_ had been
struck by two torpedoes in succession and was sinking rapidly, while
the boats were being launched with all possible speed. The women and
children were being lined up awaiting their turn. Some still clung
desperately to husbands and fathers; others clutched their children
closely to their breasts. One girl stood alone, slightly apart from
the rest. She was quite young, not more than eighteen. She did not seem
afraid, and her grave, steadfast eyes looked straight ahead.

“I beg your pardon.”

A man’s voice beside her made her start and turn. She had noticed the
speaker more than once amongst the first-class passengers. There had
been a hint of mystery about him which had appealed to her imagination.
He spoke to no one. If anyone spoke to him he was quick to rebuff the
overture. Also he had a nervous way of looking over his shoulder with a
swift, suspicious glance.

She noticed now that he was greatly agitated. There were beads of
perspiration on his brow. He was evidently in a state of overmastering
fear. And yet he did not strike her as the kind of man who would be
afraid to meet death!

“Yes?” Her grave eyes met his inquiringly.

He stood looking at her with a kind of desperate irresolution.

“It must be!” he muttered to himself. “Yes--it is the only way.” Then
aloud he said abruptly: “You are an American?”

“Yes.”

“A patriotic one?”

The girl flushed.

“I guess you’ve no right to ask such a thing! Of course I am!”

“Don’t be offended. You wouldn’t be if you knew how much there was at
stake. But I’ve got to trust some one--and it must be a woman.”

“Why?”

“Because of ‘women and children first.’” He looked round and lowered his
voice. “I’m carrying papers--vitally important papers. They may make all
the difference to the Allies in the war. You understand? These papers
have _got_ to be saved! They’ve more chance with you than with me. Will
you take them?”

The girl held out her hand.

“Wait--I must warn you. There may be a risk--if I’ve been followed. I
don’t think I have, but one never knows. If so, there will be danger.
Have you the nerve to go through with it?”

The girl smiled.

“I’ll go through with it all right. And I’m real proud to be chosen!
What am I to do with them afterwards?”

“Watch the newspapers! I’ll advertise in the personal column of the
_Times_, beginning ‘Shipmate.’ At the end of three days if there’s
nothing--well, you’ll know I’m down and out. Then take the packet to
the American Embassy, and deliver it into the Ambassador’s own hands. Is
that clear?”

“Quite clear.”

“Then be ready--I’m going to say good-bye.” He took her hand in his.
“Good-bye. Good luck to you,” he said in a louder tone.

Her hand closed on the oilskin packet that had lain in his palm.

The _Lusitania_ settled with a more decided list to starboard. In answer
to a quick command, the girl went forward to take her place in the boat.

preservation_plan.book_context: A 1915 prologue of the Lusitania hand-off is followed by the post-war comic thriller. Tommy and Tuppence form a 'joint venture'. A chance-overheard name, Jane Finn, triggers Whittington's panic, and that leads to Carter, Julius and Mr. Brown. Recurring mechanisms include: advertisements; coincidence as a theme; bluffing about how much one knows; money and marriage talk that pays off in two proposals; the hidden master criminal who uses 'Brown' and plays nonentities. Planted details pay off later: the clerk Brown, Rita, the Paris pensionnat, the Esthonia firm, the green toque, the hospital meeting and Tommy's uncle. In early chapters the girl's identity, Danvers's name and Brown's identity must not be disclosed beyond what the text shows.

essential: Date and setting: 2 p.m., May 7, 1915. The Lusitania has been torpedoed twice and is sinking, and women and children are lined up for the boats.
An unnamed young girl, no more than eighteen, stands alone and unafraid, with grave, steadfast eyes.
The man is a first-class passenger she has noticed. He is mysterious and avoids people. He glances suspiciously over his shoulder and is now agitated with fear, yet he does not seem afraid of death.
He asks whether she is American, then whether she is patriotic. She flushes indignantly ('I guess…'), which gives her American idiom.
He explains that he is carrying vitally important papers that may matter to the Allies, and that they have more chance with a woman.
He warns there may be danger if he has been followed, though he doesn't think he has. She accepts ('real proud to be chosen').
Instructions: watch for a 'Shipmate' advertisement in the Times. If nothing appears within three days, deliver the packet into the American Ambassador's own hands.
He says goodbye loudly as cover. The packet passes palm to palm, and she goes to the boat as the ship lists.
Do not name the girl or the man.
optional: Detail of women clinging to husbands and children (p1 middle).
'He spoke to no one… rebuff the overture' can be condensed into one clause.
'Quite clear' exchange (p20) and his 'Is that clear?'
The final list-to-starboard sentence can be compressed, but she must still go to the boat.

preservation_plan.voice_profile: Brisk, light omniscient narration that mostly yields to dialogue. Comedy comes from post-war slang ('old bean', 'stony', 'rag'), mock-formal narratorial labels ('Mr. Beresford magnificently', 'Miss Cowley told him'), and running jokes with setup and payoff. Tuppence is impulsive, mercenary in speech and quick at bluffing. Tommy is slow, dry and deflating. Exposition is kept spare. Suspense is planted through small, casual details: a name overheard, a clerk's name, a telephone message. Chapters often end on a cliffhanger line of dialogue. The prologue uses a graver register: plain, urgent, with short exchanges.
